claim: E122 has been fixed in tetrapod RH1 since the most recent common ancestor approximately 350 million years ago.
source: We found that E122 (codon GAA; Figure 2A) has been fixed in tetrapod RH1 since the most recent common ancestor ~350 million years ago (MYA) (Hedges et al., 2015), where it appears along the ancestral branch leading to tetrapods (Figure 2A; Table 3) following the diversification from lungfishes (I122, codon ATA, Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1) and the coelacanth (Q122, codon CAA, Figure 2A; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction analyses and phylogenetic data from the manuscript, with citation to Hedges et al., 2015 for divergence times.

claim: E122 is a key component of a hydrogen-bonding network with H211 that stabilizes the MII active-conformation.
source: E122 is a key component of an important hydrogen-bonding network with H211 that is known to stabilize the MII active-conformation (Choe et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Choe et al., 2011 structural study.

claim: E122 increases MII stability so dramatically that it is considered a functional determinant distinguishing rhodopsin from cone opsins.
source: This stability increase is so dramatic that E122 is considered a functional determinant distinguishing rhodopsin from cone opsins (Figure 1B) (Imai et al., 1997; Lamb et al., 2016; Kojima et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies (Imai et al., 1997; Lamb et al., 2016; Kojima et al., 2014) and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: The evolution of E122 likely involved a costly fitness trade-off that diminished tetrapod rod photosensitivity.
source: Paradoxically, by conferring this increase in MII stability, the evolution of E122 likely involved a costly fitness trade-off that diminished tetrapod rod photosensitivity (Yue et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yue et al., 2017 study.

claim: It is possible to improve tetrapod rod photoreceptor sensitivity by replacing E122 with Q122.
source: Indeed, it is possible to improve tetrapod rod photoreceptor sensitivity by decreasing rod dark noise in vivo by replacing E122 with a cone opsin amino acid variant (COV; Figure 1A) at site 122, such as Q122, which predominates in RH2 cone opsins (Yue et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yue et al., 2017 and Lin et al., 2017 studies.

claim: Within the Characiphysi, I122 is completely fixed.
source: Strikingly, one of the largest freshwater groups—the Characiphysi (which includes piranhas, electric eels, and catfishes [Chen et al., 2013]) —has the COV I122 residue completely fixed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data in supplementary files and figures, with citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: Fish rhodopsins show variation at site 122, including in the Coelacanth, Lungfish, and deep-sea fish lineages.
source: Interestingly, and in contrast to tetrapod rhodopsins, fish rhodopsins show variation at site 122, such as in the Coelacanth (Latimeria chalumnae), Lungfish (Neoceratodus forsteri), and deep-sea fish lineages, where COV (I, Q, M) and other residues at site 122 (V, D) are found (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Tables 1–2, Supplementary file 2) (Hunt et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 1999; Carleton et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by data in figures and tables, with citations to Hunt et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 1999; Carleton et al., 2005.

claim: Substitutions at site 122 in fish have been shown to blue-shift λMAX by up to approximately 10 nm.
source: These substitutions have been shown to blue-shift λMAX by up to ~10 nm (Hunt et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 1999)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hunt et al., 2001 and Yokoyama et al., 1999.

claim: Sites within 6 Å of site 122 displayed decreased amino acid variation in Tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1 relative to Teleost RH1.
source: Relative to Teleost RH1 (where site 122 varies), we found that sites within this radius displayed decreased amino acid variation in Tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1, where E122 and I122 are fixed, respectively (asterisks, Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by comparative analysis of amino acid variation shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is a statistically significant gene-wide increase in purifying selection within Tetrapods relative to teleosts.
source: Using likelihood ratio tests of alternative (Clade model C [(Bielawski and Yang, 2004]) and null (M2a_REL ([Weadick and Chang, 2012)]) model analyses of codon substitution rates (dN/dS) across the RH1 coding-sequence, we identified statistically significant evidence of gene-wide increases in purifying selection within Tetrapods (Table 3) and Characiphysi (Table 5) relative to teleosts ((p<0.001)).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic codon model analyses with p-values less than 0.001.

claim: There is a statistically significant gene-wide increase in purifying selection within Characiphysi relative to other teleosts.
source: Using likelihood ratio tests of alternative (Clade model C [(Bielawski and Yang, 2004]) and null (M2a_REL ([Weadick and Chang, 2012)]) model analyses of codon substitution rates (dN/dS) across the RH1 coding-sequence, we identified statistically significant evidence of gene-wide increases in purifying selection within Tetrapods (Table 3) and Characiphysi (Table 5) relative to teleosts ((p<0.001)).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic codon model analyses with p-values less than 0.001.

claim: There is a relative increase of purifying selection on site 122 codons in tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1 relative to that of teleosts.
source: Consistent with the fixation of E122 and I122 in tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1, respectively (asterisks, Figure 2C), we detected a relative increase of purifying selection on site 122 codons in tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1 relative to that of teleosts (Figure 2D; Tables 3–5)
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2D and Tables 3-5.

claim: There is significant evidence for a relative increase of purifying selection in tetrapods and the Characiphysi at RH1 sites 119, 124, and 168.
source: Yet within this radius, we found significant evidence for a relative increase of purifying selection in tetrapods and the Characiphysi (relative to teleosts) at several RH1 sites (119, 124, 168; Figure 2D; Table 4)
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses shown in Figure 2D and Table 4.

claim: Sites 119 and 168 displayed significant statistical evidence for covariation with site 122 in Teleost RH1.
source: Yet within this radius, we found significant evidence for a relative increase of purifying selection in tetrapods and the Characiphysi (relative to teleosts) at several RH1 sites (119, 124, 168; Figure 2D; Table 4), some of which (sites 119; 168) also displayed significant statistical evidence for covariation (MI) with site 122 in Teleost RH1 (Figure 2B vs. 2D; Table 4).
evidence: Supported by mutual information analyses shown in Figure 2B and Table 4.

claim: Site 119 exceeded the significance threshold in Bonferroni-corrected phylogenetic tests of correlated evolution with site 122.
source: Furthermore, one of these sites (119) also exceeded the significance threshold in our Bonferroni-corrected phylogenetic tests of correlated evolution with site 122 where p-values were calculated by performing Monte Carlo tests using data from simulations (Pagel, 1994) (Materials and methods; Table 4).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic tests of correlated evolution with Bonferroni correction, with citation to Pagel, 1994.

claim: The LEIA motif (L119-E122-I123-A124) is strongly conserved within tetrapod RH1.
source: Consistent with the entrenchment of compensatory mutations at coevolving sites (Talavera et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015), using ancestral reconstruction we found that sites 119, 122, 123, and 124 are strongly conserved as the LxxEIA (L119-E122-I123-A124; referred to as 'LEIA') and FxxINS motifs (F119-I122-N123-S124; 'FINS') within tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1, respectively
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction analyses with citations to Talavera et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015.

claim: The FINS motif (F119-I122-N123-S124) is strongly conserved within Characiphysi RH1.
source: Consistent with the entrenchment of compensatory mutations at coevolving sites (Talavera et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015), using ancestral reconstruction we found that sites 119, 122, 123, and 124 are strongly conserved as the LxxEIA (L119-E122-I123-A124; referred to as 'LEIA') and FxxINS motifs (F119-I122-N123-S124; 'FINS') within tetrapod and Characiphysi RH1, respectively
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction analyses with citations to Talavera et al., 2015; Pollock et al., 2012; Shah et al., 2015.

claim: LEIA is predicted as the ancestral Osteichthyes motif.
source: likely since the most recent common ancestor of each lineage, where LEIA is predicted as the ancestral Osteichthyes motif (Figure 3B; Tables 1, Supplementary files 1,3).
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction shown in Figure 3B and supplementary data.

claim: E122I in tetrapod RH1 blue-shifts λMAX.
source: Tetrapod RH1 with E122I (Figure 4A) and other FINS motif single substitutions to the coevolving sites (L119F, I123N, A124S; Figure 4B) displayed large shifts in rhodopsin λMAX and MII stability
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: E122I in tetrapod RH1 dramatically destabilizes the MII active-conformation.
source: Tetrapod RH1 with E122I (Figure 4A) and other FINS motif single substitutions to the coevolving sites (L119F, I123N, A124S; Figure 4B) displayed large shifts in rhodopsin λMAX and MII stability
evidence: Supported by experimental fluorescence-based measurements of MII stability shown in Figure 4A.

claim: L119F significantly increases the stability of the active-conformation and red-shifts λMAX.
source: with two single mutations (L119F, A124S) significantly increasing the stability of the active-conformation but producing opposite spectral tuning effects (Figure 4B; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Table 6.

claim: A124S significantly increases the stability of the active-conformation and blue-shifts λMAX.
source: with two single mutations (L119F, A124S) significantly increasing the stability of the active-conformation but producing opposite spectral tuning effects (Figure 4B; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Table 6.

claim: I123N destabilizes the active-conformation almost as dramatically as E122I but produces no spectral tuning effect.
source: Meanwhile, I123N destabilized the active-conformation almost as dramatically as E122I but produced no spectral tuning effect (Figure 4B; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Table 6.

claim: The L119F/I123N/A124S triple mutation fully restores the MII stability of E122I tetrapod rhodopsin to wild-type levels.
source: We found, incredibly, that the L119F/I123N/A124S triple mutation fully restored the MII stability of E122I tetrapod rhodopsin to WT levels, while even further blue-shifting λMAX relative to E122I (Figure 4E; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Table 6.

claim: The L119F/E122I/I123N/A124S quadruple mutant further blue-shifts λMAX relative to E122I.
source: We found, incredibly, that the L119F/I123N/A124S triple mutation fully restored the MII stability of E122I tetrapod rhodopsin to WT levels, while even further blue-shifting λMAX relative to E122I (Figure 4E; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Table 6.

claim: The LEIA and FINS motifs are convergent solutions for high tetrapod RH1 MII stability but with different spectral sensitivities.
source: The LEIA and FINS motifs are therefore two configurations conferring convergent MII stabilities but different spectral sensitivities, with the blue-shifting I122-containing FINS motif likely also decreasing rod dark noise in vivo (Gozem et al., 2012; Yue et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to Gozem et al., 2012 and Yue et al., 2017.

claim: N123 is not observed within any vertebrate rhodopsin other than the Characiphysi.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that N123, which is not, to our knowledge, observed within any vertebrate rhodopsin other than the Characiphysi (Tables 12, Supplementary files 1–3) is nevertheless required for a complete rescue of MII stability within the LWS COV I122 background
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data in tables and supplementary files.

claim: N123 is required for a complete rescue of MII stability within the I122 background.
source: Our experiments demonstrate that N123, which is not, to our knowledge, observed within any vertebrate rhodopsin other than the Characiphysi (Tables 12, Supplementary files 1–3) is nevertheless required for a complete rescue of MII stability within the LWS COV I122 background
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that the quadruple mutant with N123 fully rescues MII stability.

claim: N123 has opposite functional effects depending on E vs. I122 backgrounds (sign-epistasis).
source: where it has opposite functional effects depending on E vs. I122 backgrounds (also known as sign-epistasis [Storz, 2016; Weinreich et al., 2006]) (Figure 4D–E; Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4D-E and Figure 5, with citations to Storz, 2016 and Weinreich et al., 2006.

claim: Cone opsins have low MII stability and rapidly release all-trans retinal.
source: Cone opsins have low MII stability and therefore rapidly release atRAL (Imai et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2012a)
evidence: Supported by citations to Imai et al., 1997 and Chen et al., 2012a.

claim: Rods regenerate thousands of times slower than cones after bright-light exposure.
source: Rods, in contrast, regenerate thousands of times slower than cones after bright-light exposure (Mata et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mata et al., 2002.

claim: Rod exposure to bright flashes of light leads to all-trans retinal release that can outpace clearance by visual cycle enzymes.
source: Indeed, rod exposure to bright flashes of light leads to atRAL release that can outpace clearance by visual cycle enzymes (Sommer et al., 2014; Rózanowska and Sarna, 2005), thus leading to accumulation (Saari et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2010) and light-induced retinopathy through various modes of cellular toxicity involving oxidative stress (Maeda et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sommer et al., 2014; Rózanowska and Sarna, 2005; Saari et al., 1998; Lee et al., 2010; Maeda et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012b.

claim: MII may play a role in retinal photoprotection by complexing with arrestin after Gt signaling to re-uptake toxic all-trans retinal after rod photobleaching.
source: Interestingly, recent biochemical evidence suggests MII may play a role in retinal photoprotection by complexing with arrestin after Gt signaling to re-uptake and thus provide a sink for toxic atRAL after rod photobleaching (Sommer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommer et al., 2014.

claim: The evolution of rhodopsin's high conformational selectivity for toxic all-trans retinal may be a functional specialization.
source: This suggests the evolution of rhodopsin's high conformational selectivity for toxic atRAL may be a functional specialization (Schafer et al., 2016; Schafer and Farrens, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Schafer et al., 2016 and Schafer and Farrens, 2015.

claim: Slowing the rate of rhodopsin regeneration is one of the most promising strategies to increase retinal resistance to photodamage.
source: First, one of the most promising strategies to increase retinal resistance to photodamage is to slow the rate of rhodopsin regeneration, which can be achieved via mutations or molecules inhibiting the normal functioning of visual cycle proteins responsible for synthesizing 11-cis retinal (11CR) (Wenzel et al., 2001; Saari et al., 2001; Mandal et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wenzel et al., 2001; Saari et al., 2001; Mandal et al., 2011.

claim: Rhodopsins with high MII stability tend to have slowed 11-cis retinal regeneration rates.
source: These observations suggest that rhodopsin conformational selectivity may be an overlooked functional specialization of dim-light vision—one that may be associated with rates of regeneration and therefore photoprotection in the eye. Although multiple molecular mechanisms within the visual cycle appear to have evolved to prevent the accumulation of toxic atRAL (Rózanowska and Sarna, 2005; Chen et al., 2012c) as well as excess 11CR (Quazi and Molday, 2014, a possible role for rhodopsin's intrinsic conformational selectivity in sequestering these retinal ligands has been mostly overlooked. Recent advances in rhodopsin biochemistry suggest that such a photoprotective mechanism may indeed exist. In contrast to cones, which have an expanded retinoid recycling capacity (Wang and Kefalov, 2011; Tsybovsky and Palczewski, 2015), in rods atRAL clearance is limited by the activity of retinal dehydrogenases (RDH) (Saari et al., 1998; Chen et al., 2012b; Chen et al., 2012c), and can transiently accumulate to toxic levels (Sommer et al., 2014 causing light induced-retinopathy through a variety of mechanisms involving oxidative stress (Maeda et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2012b. Unlike cone opsins, which have low active-conformation stability, the rhodopsin active-conformation is highly stable due in large part to the evolution of E122 (Imai et al., 1997), and when phosphorylated and bound to rod arrestin, contains a binding affinity for atRAL sufficient for sequestration and reduction below toxic levels (Sommer et al., 2014; Rózanowska and Sarna, 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies including Imai et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2012a.

claim: Elevated all-trans retinal concentrations increase all-trans retinal re-uptake by active-conformation rhodopsin in vitro.
source: Indeed, it is now known that elevated atRAL concentrations will increase atRAL re-uptake by active-conformation rhodopsin in vitro (Schafer et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Schafer et al., 2016.

claim: The only natural intermediate between the wild-type tetrapod consensus motif (LEIA) and the wild-type Characiphysi motif (FINS) is FIIA from Lungfish RH1.
source: The only natural intermediate between the wild-type tetrapod consensus motif (LEIA) and the wild-type Characiphysi motif (FINS) is 'FIIA' from Lungfish RH1.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data and ancestral reconstruction shown in Figure 5.

claim: The selective constraints on E122 are repeatedly relaxed within the constant darkness of deep-dwelling fish environments.
source: Specifically, our results demonstrate that the only visual ecologies where the selective constraints on E122 are repeatedly relaxed across the phylogeny is within the constant darkness of deep-dwelling fish environments (Hunt et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 1999)—the natural system where one might expect the fitness effects of the rhodopsin-mediated trade-off between photosensitivity and photoprotection to drastically shift, as there is likely little photodamage risk for fishes living below 1000 m in near-permanent darkness (Denton, 1990).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data and citations to Hunt et al., 2001; Yokoyama et al., 1999; Denton, 1990.

claim: All whales strictly maintain E122.
source: All whales by contrast—some of which routinely dive into complete darkness at depths near 2000 m (e.g. the sperm whale) (Denton, 1990; Watkins et al., 1993)—strictly maintain E122
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic data and citations to Denton, 1990 and Watkins et al., 1993.

claim: HEK293T cells were authenticated by STR profiling.
source: HEK293T cells were obtained from David Hampson (University of Toronto), were authenticated by STR profiling (Centre for Applied Genomics, The Hospital for Sick Children) and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: HEK293T cells tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
source: HEK293T cells were obtained from David Hampson (University of Toronto), were authenticated by STR profiling (Centre for Applied Genomics, The Hospital for Sick Children) and tested negative for mycoplasma contamination.
evidence: Explicitly stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: Wild-type bovine rhodopsin has a λMAX of 498.2 ± 0.1 nm.
source: Wild-type Bovine rhodopsin LEIA 498.2 ± 0.1 (4)
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: E122I mutation shifts λMAX to 495.4 ± 0.2 nm.
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: L119F mutation shifts λMAX to 503.5 ± 0.8 nm.
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: I123N mutation does not significantly change λMAX (498.0 ± 0.3 nm).
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: A124S mutation shifts λMAX to 496.6 ± 0.2 nm.
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: The L119F/E122I/I123N/A124S quadruple mutant has a λMAX of 492.6 ± 0.3 nm.
evidence: Supported by experimental spectroscopic measurements shown in Table 6.

claim: Trade-offs between protein stability and activity can restrict access to evolutionary trajectories.
source: Trade-offs between protein stability and activity can restrict access to evolutionary trajectories, but widespread epistasis may facilitate indirect routes to adaptation.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a general principle.

claim: High MII stability could have likely evolved without E122.
source: Here, we demonstrate that high MII stability could have likely evolved without E122, but instead, selection appears to have entrenched E122 in tetrapods via epistatic interactions with nearby coevolving sites.
evidence: Supported by experimental demonstration that the FINS motif achieves high MII stability without E122.

claim: Selection appears to have entrenched E122 in tetrapods via epistatic interactions with nearby coevolving sites.
source: Here, we demonstrate that high MII stability could have likely evolved without E122, but instead, selection appears to have entrenched E122 in tetrapods via epistatic interactions with nearby coevolving sites.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses showing increased purifying selection and coevolution patterns.

claim: Within tetrapods, E122 and high MII stability cannot be sacrificed—not even for improvements to rod photosensitivity.
source: Our results suggest that within tetrapods, E122 and high MII stability cannot be sacrificed—not even for improvements to rod photosensitivity.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: In fishes, selection may have exploited epistatic effects to explore alternative trajectories via indirect routes with low MII stability.
source: In fishes by contrast, selection may have exploited these epistatic effects to explore alternative trajectories, but via indirect routes with low MII stability.
evidence: Stated in the abstract as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The transition period in vertebrate evolution when E122 was fixed is characterized by extensive morphological modifications for vision within terrestrial environments.
source: This transition period in vertebrate evolution is characterized by extensive morphological modifications for vision within terrestrial environments, and likely included large increases in environmental light irradiance (MacIver et al., 2017; Warrant and Johnsen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacIver et al., 2017 and Warrant and Johnsen, 2013.

claim: The transition period in vertebrate evolution when E122 was fixed likely included large increases in environmental light irradiance.
source: This transition period in vertebrate evolution is characterized by extensive morphological modifications for vision within terrestrial environments, and likely included large increases in environmental light irradiance (MacIver et al., 2017; Warrant and Johnsen, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacIver et al., 2017 and Warrant and Johnsen, 2013.

claim: Within the Characiphysi, I122 was introduced likely through E122I mutation.
source: Within this group, the COV residue I122 was introduced likely through E122I (codon ATC; Figure 2A), where I122 is now completely fixed across the extant Characiphysi (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by ancestral reconstruction shown in Figure 2A and phylogenetic data.

claim: Sites 119, 123 have been previously found capable of functionally compensating for human pathogenic mutations disrupting the MII-stabilizing E122-H211 interaction.
source: This is within the range at which intramolecular forces such as Van der Waals and hydrophobic interactions between amino acids are thought to occur (Ivankov et al., 2014). It is known, however, that there is a tendency of covariation analyses such as MI to identify coevolving sites proximal to each other, which may in turn overlook more distal coevolving sites potentially indirectly interacting with site 122 (Talavera et al., 2015). Nevertheless, sites detected within this 6 Å radius (sites 119, 123) have been previously found capable of functionally compensating for human pathogenic mutations (e.g. A164V) disrupting the MII-stabilizing E122-H211 interaction (Stojanovic et al., 2003)
evidence: Supported by citation to Stojanovic et al., 2003.

claim: Decreases in amino acid variation observed in tetrapods and Characiphysi at sites near 122 are driven by an increase in purifying selection on non-synonymous codons.
source: Furthermore, we hypothesized that decreases in amino acid variation observed in these lineages would be driven by an increase in purifying selection on non-synonymous codons, ultimately reflecting the entrenchment of compensatory amino acid residues by natural selection.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses of dN/dS ratios.

claim: An increase in purifying selection on non-synonymous codons drove the reduction in amino acid variation at positions coevolving with site 122.
source: Taken together, these results provide evidence that an increase in purifying selection on non-synonymous codons drove the reduction in amino acid variation at positions coevolving with site 122, and this likely accompanied the fixation of E122 and I122 in tetrapods and the Characiphysi, respectively.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses of dN/dS ratios and coevolution patterns.

claim: The reduction in amino acid variation at coevolving sites likely accompanied the fixation of E122 and I122 in tetrapods and the Characiphysi, respectively.
source: Taken together, these results provide evidence that an increase in purifying selection on non-synonymous codons drove the reduction in amino acid variation at positions coevolving with site 122, and this likely accompanied the fixation of E122 and I122 in tetrapods and the Characiphysi, respectively.
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analyses showing temporal correlation between fixation and increased purifying selection.

claim: FINS substitutions at coevolving sites could functionally compensate for some of the pleiotropic effects of E122I on tetrapod rhodopsin.
source: This suggested that FINS substitutions at coevolving sites could functionally compensate for some of the pleiotropic effects of E122I on tetrapod rhodopsin.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing partial rescue effects of individual FINS mutations.

claim: None of the partial FINS motif intermediates were sufficient to restore wild-type levels of MII stability within the I122 background.
source: We created double and triple mutants representing partial replacements of the LEIA with the FINS motif, which tended to blue-shift λMAX (Figure 4C–D; Table 6). Yet, none of these intermediates were sufficient to restore WT-levels of MII stability within the COV I122 background (Figure 4C–D; Table 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4C-D and Table 6.

claim: The complete recapitulation of the FINS motif within tetrapod rhodopsin is required for a full restoration of wild-type active-conformation stability.
source: We therefore reasoned that the complete recapitulation of the FINS motif within tetrapod rhodopsin may be required for a full restoration of WT active-conformation stability.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that only the quadruple mutant fully rescues MII stability.

claim: The FINS motif mediates a series of context-dependent structural rearrangements promoting novel interactions.
source: Structural analysis of a homology model of the MII active-state structure (Materials and methods; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggests the conformation of the FINS motif mediates a series of context-dependent structural rearrangements promoting novel interactions (F119 with W161; N123 with N78/T160; Figure 5—figure supplement 1) that can interact with existing GPCR hydrogen bond networks known to stabilize the MII active conformation (S124 with D83-S298- N302; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; [Choe et al., 2011]).
evidence: Supported by homology modeling analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Patterns of naturally occurring sequence variation can be used to successfully navigate a complex sequence-function landscape to engineer the spectral and non-spectral functions of rhodopsin simultaneously.
source: These epistatic structural interactions produce correspondingly variable pleiotropic effects on RH1 spectral absorbance and MII stability (Figure 4), which were consistent with patterns of natural sequence variation at these positions across vertebrate rhodopsins. Using these patterns of naturally occurring sequence variation, we could successfully navigate a complex sequence-function landscape (Figure 5) to engineer the spectral and non-spectral functions of rhodopsin simultaneously.
evidence: Supported by experimental demonstration that natural variation patterns guided successful protein engineering.

claim: The sign-epistasis of site 123 may have constrained tetrapod RH1 to the local fitness optima of E122 and the LEIA motif.
source: Detrimental intermediates and historical contingency (Pál and Papp, 2017; Wu et al., 2016; Starr et al., 2017; Weinreich et al., 2006; Palmer et al., 2015) may ultimately explain why the road to the FINS motif was less travelled by in evolutionary history; although tetrapods could have in theory evolved both higher rod photosensitivity and high MII stability via the FINS motif (Gozem et al., 2012; Yue et al., 2017; Imai et al., 1997), the sign-epistasis of site 123 (Figure 4) may have constrained tetrapod RH1 to the local fitness optima of E122 and the LEIA motif (Storz, 2016; Weinreich et al., 2005; Poelwijk et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to evolutionary theory papers.

claim: E122 as a historical contingency may have promoted MII-mediated photoprotection within terrestrial environments.
source: E122 as a historical contingency may have promoted MII-mediated photoprotection within terrestrial environments and was therefore entrenched by purifying selection pressures and epistatic interactions with nearby sites (Pollock et al., 2012; Goldstein and Pollock, 2017; Shah et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental and phylogenetic data, with citations to entrenchment theory.

claim: E122 may be a 'molecular springboard' for reaching higher levels of MII stability and photoprotection that COV could not potentiate.
source: E122 may therefore be a 'molecular springboard' (Pál and Papp, 2017 for reaching higher levels of MII stability and photoprotection that COV could not potentiate (Dungan and Chang, 2017; Hauser et al., 2017b; Gutierrez et al., 2018)
evidence: Speculative inference with citations to Pál and Papp, 2017; Dungan and Chang, 2017; Hauser et al., 2017b; Gutierrez et al., 2018.

claim: E122/S124 is nearly six-fold more stable than I122/S124.
source: indeed, E122/S124 is nearly six-fold more stable than I122/S124 (Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Temporal and spatial variation in fish visual ecologies may have opened up indirect trajectories containing low MII stability created by the epistasis of the coevolutionary network.
source: By contrast, temporal and spatial variation in fish visual ecologies (Hauser and Chang, 2017a; Bowmaker, 2008 may have opened up the indirect trajectories containing low MII stability (Pál and Papp, 2017; Ogbunugafor et al., 2016; Steinberg and Ostermeier, 2016 created by the epistasis of the coevolutionary network (Wu et al., 2016; Palmer et al., 2015)
evidence: Speculative inference with citations to multiple studies on visual ecology and evolutionary theory.

claim: Selection has allowed multiple fish lineages to innovate at this coevolving network through amino acid variation that may promote photosensitivity instead of MII stability.

claim: Changing environmental constraints within the ancestral Characiphysi population may have bridged the evolutionary valleys between the LEIA and FINS motifs.
source: Although speculative, this implies that changing environmental constraints within the ancestral Characiphysi population (Chen et al., 2013) may have bridged the evolutionary valleys between the LEIA and FINS motifs, as has been observed in some experimental studies on bacterial enzymes mediating antibiotic resistance (Ogbunugafor et al., 2016; Steinberg and Ostermeier, 2016).
evidence: Speculative inference with citations to Chen et al., 2013; Ogbunugafor et al., 2016; Steinberg and Ostermeier, 2016.

source: Second, this further argues that novel sequence-function solutions in proteins (McMurrough et al., 2014; Mateu and Fersht, 1999; Tarvin et al., 2017) can be discovered by integrating genetic and ecological information to reveal ancient evolutionary trajectories (Liebeskind et al., 2015; McTavish et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by the study's approach and citations to related work.

claim: The accuracy of computational models remains limited to describing changes in protein stability, rather than adaptive shifts in protein function and trade-offs with stability.
source: These evolutionary solutions may be otherwise unpredictable from biophysical perspectives (Starr and Thornton, 2017; Sailer and Harms, 2017; Otwinowski and Plotkin, 2014) where the accuracy of computational models remains limited to describing changes in protein stability (Goldenzweig and Fleishman, 2018; Echave et al., 2016; Goldstein and Pollock, 2017), rather than the adaptive shifts in protein function and trade-offs with stability—a scenario likely widespread in natural systems (Pál and Papp, 2017; McMurrough et al., 2014; Mateu and Fersht, 1999; Tarvin et al., 2017; DePristo et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple computational and evolutionary studies.
